front.title: An Information Model and JSON Encoding for Certificate Observation Records
front.workgroup: Operations and Management Area Working Group

abstract.t: Operators need to know which X.509 certificates are installed where, when they expire, and whether a renewed certificate has actually reached the service that uses it. This information is produced by many different parties: network observers, local agents, configuration management systems, and certificate issuers. Each currently uses its own format, and many endpoints cannot be reached by a central monitoring system at all.

This document defines the Certificate Observation Record: a transport-independent information model describing one certificate as seen at one location by one reporter, together with a JSON encoding, an HTTP-based exchange mechanism, and a file-based handoff. The record distinguishes the reporter from the subject it describes, so that one system can report on behalf of endpoints that a collector cannot reach, and it labels each record with the kind of evidence it carries, so that a collector can detect when issuance, deployment and actual service diverge.

note.name: About This Document
note.t: Discussion of this document is expected to take place on the Operations and Management Area Working Group mailing list (opsawg@ietf.org). Feedback on the ACME and LAMPS lists is also welcome where relevant.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The maximum validity of publicly trusted TLS server certificates is being reduced in stages, reaching 47 days in 2029 . Many organisations apply similar or shorter lifetimes to certificates from private certification authorities. As lifetimes shrink, certificate renewal must be automated, and the failure modes move: issuance usually succeeds, but the new certificate is not installed on every endpoint, is installed but not loaded by the service, or is installed on a system that no monitoring tool examines.

Automated issuance protocols such as ACME and ACME Renewal Information tell a client when to renew. They do not tell an operator whether the result reached every place where it is needed. Certificate Transparency records publicly trusted issuance but not deployment, and does not cover private certification authorities.
In practice, knowledge about certificates is spread across several systems:

ul.li: network observers that connect to a service and record the certificate it presents;
local agents that read certificates from files, platform certificate stores or application key stores;
issuer systems, such as certification authorities and ACME servers, that know what was issued and when renewal is due.

section.t: Each of these uses its own data format, so correlating them requires custom integration for every pair of tools. In addition, a large class of certificates is invisible to network observation: endpoints in isolated network segments, services that only accept mutually authenticated TLS, intermittently connected devices, and certificates that are never presented on a listening port at all, such as client certificates, signing certificates and certificates waiting on disk to be loaded.
This document defines a common record format so that any of these parties can describe what it knows about a certificate, and any collector can consume and correlate those descriptions. It specifies:

ul.li: an information model for a Certificate Observation Record ();
a JSON encoding, with a CDDL definition ();
an HTTP push and pull binding, and a file-based handoff ();
guidance on how collectors correlate records ().

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document covers X.509 certificates used by any protocol, not only TLS. It does not define how certificates are requested, issued, renewed or installed, and it does not define alerting policy. A record describes a certificate; it never carries private key material.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: A statement, made by one Reporter at one point in time, about one certificate (or the absence of an expected certificate) at one Location of one Subject.
The system that produces a record. A Reporter may describe itself or another system.
The system or service that the record is about. The Subject is the entity under which a Collector files the record.
The case where the Reporter and the Subject are different systems, for example a configuration management system reporting on an endpoint it manages.
Where on the Subject the certificate was found or is expected: a network endpoint, a file, a certificate store entry, or a configuration item.
How the Reporter came to know the information in the record (see ).

A system that receives records from Reporters, stores them, and correlates them. A monitoring system, a certificate lifecycle management system or a security information system can act as a Collector.
A Reporter that learns about certificates by connecting to a network service and examining what it presents.
A Reporter running on the Subject that reads certificates from local files, platform certificate stores or application key stores.
A system that holds the desired configuration of managed endpoints and deploys files and settings to them.
A certification authority, registration authority or automated issuance server (for example an ACME server) that can report what it issued.

section.name: Network Observation
section.t: A network observer periodically connects to known services, completes a TLS handshake, and records the presented certificate and chain. This is the most common form of certificate monitoring today. It shows what clients actually receive, but only for services the observer can reach and authenticate to.

section.name: Endpoints Not Reachable by the Collector
section.t: Many endpoints cannot be reached by a central observer: systems in isolated or perimeter network segments, services listening only on local interfaces, services that require client authentication, intermittently connected devices, and remote sites. A local agent on such an endpoint reads its certificates and sends records outbound to a Collector, or places them where an existing agent forwards them. Only one outbound path from the endpoint is required.

section.name: Reporting by a Configuration Management System
section.t: A configuration management system often has access to endpoints that the Collector cannot reach, and knows which certificate each endpoint is supposed to hold. It can report, on behalf of each managed endpoint, what it declared and what it deployed, and it can run collection tasks on the endpoint and report the observed result. The Collector files these records under the managed endpoint, not under the configuration management system.

section.name: Issuer Reporting
section.t: An issuer system reports each certificate it issues, with its validity period and, where available, the renewal window suggested by ACME Renewal Information . This gives the Collector the expected state against which deployments can be compared.

section.name: Deployment Verification
section.t: By comparing records about the same Subject and Location that carry different evidence types, a Collector can detect common failures: a certificate issued but never deployed, deployed to disk but not loaded by the service, or loaded on one node of a cluster but not on the others.

section.name: Certificates Not Presented on a Network Port
section.t: Client certificates, signing certificates, certification authority certificates, and certificates used only inside an application are never seen by a network observer. Local agents and configuration management systems can report them with the same record format.

section.name: Appliances and Constrained Devices
section.t: Many network appliances, printers and management controllers cannot run an issuance client or a local agent and expose only limited management interfaces. The information model is designed so that it can be mapped to such interfaces in the future (see ), while proxy reporting by a configuration management system covers these devices in the meantime.

section.name: Information Model
section.t: A Certificate Observation Record contains the following elements. Element names here are abstract; their JSON names are given in .

dl.dd: The version of the record format. This document defines version 1.
An identifier chosen by the Reporter, unique per Reporter, that allows a Collector to detect duplicate deliveries.
A stable identifier of the Reporter, such as a fully qualified domain name or a URI.

Identifies the system the record is about: a host name, a service name, and/or an opaque identifier assigned by the operator. At least one of these MUST be present. When the Reporter describes itself, the subject identifies the Reporter.

Where the certificate is used or stored on the Subject: a network address, port and server name indication value; a file path; a certificate store and entry label; or a configuration item name. At least one element MUST be present.
How the information was obtained ().
The time at which the Reporter obtained the information.
The number of seconds after observed-at during which the Reporter considers the record current. A Collector treats a record as stale after this period ().

A description of the certificate: its SHA-256 fingerprint (mandatory within this element), subject and issuer distinguished names, subject alternative names, serial number, validity period, public key algorithm and size, and signature algorithm. The DER encoding of the certificate MAY be included. This element MUST be present unless the record reports that an expected certificate was not found.
The fingerprints of the intermediate certificates presented or stored with the certificate, the result of path validation as performed by the Reporter, and the trust anchor used.
The SHA-256 fingerprint of the certificate that the Reporter believes should be at this Location, for example as declared by a configuration management system.
The start and end of the period in which renewal is suggested, for example as obtained from ACME Renewal Information.
A list of conditions the Reporter detected ().
Additional elements defined by future specifications or by private agreement. Collectors MUST ignore extensions they do not understand.

section.name: Evidence Types
section.t: The evidence type allows a Collector to weigh and compare records. This document defines the following values:

dl.dd: An issuer system issued this certificate for this Subject and Location.
The configuration of the Subject states that this certificate should be at this Location. No deployment or observation is implied.
A deployment action that placed this certificate at this Location completed successfully. The Reporter did not verify that the service loaded it.
The Reporter read the certificate from a file, a platform certificate store or an application key store on the Subject.
The Reporter obtained the certificate from a protocol exchange with the Subject, such as a TLS handshake.

section.t: A Reporter MUST use the evidence type that reflects how it actually obtained the information, and MUST NOT report "observed-store" or "observed-wire" for information derived only from configuration or deployment results. Additional values can be registered ().

section.name: Status Values
section.t: A Reporter MAY include one or more of the following status values. Their absence does not imply that the certificate is valid.

dl.dd: No certificate was found at the Location.
The current time is after the certificate's notAfter.
The current time is before the certificate's notBefore.
Path validation by the Reporter failed.
The certificate does not match the name used to reach the service.
The fingerprint differs from the expected fingerprint.

section.t: Thresholds such as "expiring soon" are policy decisions and are left to the Collector.

section.name: JSON Encoding
section.t: Records are encoded as JSON objects. One or more records are carried in a record set. Timestamps are RFC 3339 date-time values in UTC. Fingerprints are lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 digests of the DER-encoded certificate. The structure is defined by the following CDDL :

The "der" member, when present, contains the base64 encoding of the DER-encoded certificate. The "public-key-algorithm" and "signature-algorithm" members contain human-readable algorithm names; a future revision may reference an algorithm registry instead.

section.name: Example: Proxy Reporting by a Configuration Management System
section.t: A configuration management system reports, on behalf of a printer that the Collector cannot reach, that it deployed a certificate. A second record, produced by a collection task the system ran on the printer's management interface, reports that the old certificate is still being served.

section.name: HTTP Push
section.t: A Reporter sends a record set to a Collector using an HTTP POST request to a URI configured by the operator. The request content MUST be a cert-observation-set with media type "application/cert-observation+json" (). HTTPS MUST be used.
The Collector responds as follows:

ul.li: 202 (Accepted) when the record set was accepted for processing;
400 (Bad Request) when the content is not a valid record set;
415 (Unsupported Media Type) when the media type or version is not supported.

section.t: A Collector MAY accept part of a record set and reject records for Subjects the Reporter is not authorised to report on; it then SHOULD return 202 and indicate the rejected records using a problem details object . Reporters SHOULD retry failed deliveries with exponential back-off and SHOULD include record identifiers so that retries do not create duplicates.

section.name: HTTP Pull
section.t: A Reporter MAY instead publish its current record set at an HTTPS URI, which a Collector retrieves with GET. The Reporter SHOULD provide an entity tag so that the Collector can use conditional requests. Pull requires the Collector to reach the Reporter and is therefore not suitable for the use case in ; push or file handoff should be used there.

section.name: File-Based Handoff
section.t: Many endpoints already run a monitoring or log forwarding agent that transports local files to a central system. A Reporter MAY write record sets as files to a directory configured for such an agent. Each file contains one cert-observation-set and SHOULD use the file name extension ".cor.json". Reporters MUST write files atomically, for example by writing to a temporary name and renaming, so that a partially written file is never forwarded.

section.name: Correlation
section.t: A Collector groups records by Subject and Location. Within a group, it compares certificate fingerprints across evidence types. The following comparisons are useful; the resulting alerts are a matter of local policy:

ul.li: a newer "issued" or "declared" fingerprint with no matching "deployed" record: the certificate was not distributed;
any record with an expected fingerprint that differs from the reported one.

section.t: Location elements can be described differently by different Reporters. Collectors SHOULD allow operators to define equivalences, for example between a file path and the network port that serves it.

section.name: Freshness
section.t: A record whose observed-at plus valid-for is in the past is stale. A Collector MUST NOT treat a stale record as evidence that a certificate is currently present, and SHOULD alert when a Subject that previously reported stops reporting. This prevents a failed Reporter, for example a configuration management run that no longer executes, from hiding an expiring certificate behind its last successful report.
When valid-for is absent, the Collector applies a locally configured default.

section.name: Other Bindings
section.t: The information model in is independent of transport. Future documents may define:

ul.li: a YANG data model, so that network devices can expose records through existing management protocols;
a CBOR encoding for constrained devices.

section.t: The relationship to cryptographic inventories of software artifacts, which describe algorithms and keys embedded in software rather than certificates observed in operation, is also for further study.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: [RFC Editor: please remove this section before publication, together with the reference to RFC 7942.]
This section records the status of known implementations of the protocol defined by this specification at the time of posting of this Internet-Draft, and is based on a proposal described in .

No implementations are known at the time of writing. The author plans a prototype consisting of a local agent and a configuration management task that produce records, and an exporter for an open-source monitoring system that consumes them.

section.name: Reporter Authentication and Authorisation
section.t: A false record can hide a problem: a forged "observed-wire" record with a valid certificate could suppress an expiry alert until the service fails. Collectors MUST authenticate Reporters, for example using TLS client certificates or bearer tokens over HTTPS, and MUST maintain an authorisation policy that states which Subjects each Reporter may report on. By default, a Reporter SHOULD only be authorised to report on itself; proxy reporting SHOULD require explicit configuration.

Where records pass through intermediaries such as file-forwarding agents, the Collector authenticates the agent rather than the Reporter. Deployments that need end-to-end integrity MAY sign record sets using JSON Web Signature ; the details are left for a future revision.

section.name: Replay and Staleness
section.t: An attacker who can replay old records could make a Collector believe a certificate is still in place. The freshness rules in limit the effect of replay. Collectors SHOULD reject records whose observed-at lies significantly in the future and SHOULD discard duplicate record identifiers from the same Reporter.

section.name: Information Disclosure
section.t: A collection of records is a detailed map of an organisation's services, internal names, certification authorities and weak algorithms, which is valuable to an attacker. Records MUST be transmitted only over authenticated, encrypted channels, and Collectors SHOULD protect stored records accordingly. Files written for file-based handoff SHOULD be readable only by the forwarding agent.

section.name: Private Keys
section.t: Records describe certificates only. A Reporter MUST NOT include private keys or any secret key material in a record, including in extensions.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Client certificates and some server certificates contain personal data such as names and email addresses. Reporters SHOULD omit the subject distinguished name, subject alternative names and DER encoding of certificates that identify individuals unless the operator needs them, and rely on the fingerprint for correlation.
